stem: Which of these is a **biological** component of an ecosystem?

options.content: Light
options.rationale: Light is a physical (non-living) component.

options.content: Temperature
options.rationale: Temperature is a physical component.

options.content: Water in the soil
options.rationale: Water is a physical component, even though organisms need it.

options.content: Earthworms in the soil
options.rationale: Earthworms are living organisms, so they are a biological component.

explanation: Biological (biotic) components are the living organisms: producers, consumers and decomposers. Light, temperature, water, air and soil particles are physical components.

stem: Which statement best describes an **ecosystem**?

options.content: All the organisms of one species living together in an area
options.rationale: That is a population.

options.content: A community of organisms together with their physical environment
options.rationale: An ecosystem includes both the living organisms and the non-living surroundings.

options.content: The place where an organism lives
options.rationale: That is a habitat.

options.content: All the plants growing in an area, with the soil they grow in
options.rationale: Plants are only part of the community; an ecosystem also includes animals, decomposers and the physical environment.

explanation: An ecosystem is a self-contained unit of interdependent organisms (the community) and their physical environment, such as Lake Kariba or an area of msasa woodland.

stem: Name the dark, partly decomposed organic matter found in soil.

rejected.feedback: Litter is undecayed dead material on the surface. Once it has partly decomposed in the soil it is called humus.
Leaf litter is undecayed dead material on the surface. Once it has partly decomposed in the soil it is called humus.
Clay is a mineral part of soil, made of tiny rock particles. The decayed organic matter is humus.
Compost is made by people from decaying plant waste and adds humus to the soil; the material in soil itself is called humus.

explanation: Humus forms when decomposers partly break down dead leaves, roots, animals and dung. It holds water, binds soil particles into crumbs and slowly releases mineral ions.
hints: Compost and manure add it to soil.

stem: True or false: water drains through clay soil faster than through sandy soil.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not so: clay particles are tiny and leave tiny pores, so water drains through clay slowly. Water drains fastest through sandy soil, which has large particles and large pores.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: water drains slowly through clay because its tiny particles leave tiny pores. Sandy soil, with large pores, drains fastest.

explanation: Large sand particles leave large spaces through which water drains quickly. Tiny clay particles leave tiny spaces that hold water and let it through slowly, so clay can become waterlogged.
hints: Think about the size of the spaces between the particles.

stem: Which type of soil is made mostly of the **largest** mineral particles?

options.content: Clay soil
options.rationale: Clay particles are the smallest, less than 0.002 mm across.

options.content: Silty soil
options.rationale: Silt particles are medium-sized, between clay and sand.

options.content: Sandy soil
options.rationale: Sand particles are the largest soil particles, up to about 2 mm across.

options.content: Loam
options.rationale: Loam is a mixture of sand, silt and clay, so it is not mostly the largest particles.

explanation: Soil particles are classified by size: sand is the largest, then silt, and clay is the smallest. A sandy soil is made mostly of sand particles.

stem: How do earthworms improve the soil for crops?

options.content: Their burrows let in air and water, and they mix dead leaves in
options.rationale: Burrowing aerates and drains the soil; dragging leaves underground adds organic matter.

options.content: They fix nitrogen from the air into nitrates in the soil
options.rationale: Nitrogen fixation is done by some bacteria, not by earthworms.

options.content: They photosynthesise and add sugars to the soil
options.rationale: Earthworms are animals; they cannot photosynthesise.

options.content: They kill the bacteria that cause dead leaves to decay
options.rationale: Decay by bacteria releases nutrients; earthworms help it by breaking litter into small pieces.

explanation: Earthworm burrows aerate the soil and help water drain. Earthworms pull dead leaves underground, mix the soil layers and break litter into small pieces that decomposers can work on quickly.

stem: A soil sample is shaken with water in a measuring cylinder and left to settle overnight. Which material is found **floating** on the surface of the water?

options.content: Clay
options.rationale: The finest clay stays suspended, making the water cloudy, and slowly settles on top of the sediment.

options.content: Coarse sand
options.rationale: Coarse sand is heavy and settles first, at the bottom.

options.content: Silt
options.rationale: Silt settles in a layer above the sand.

options.content: Humus
options.rationale: Humus is light organic matter and floats.

explanation: Particles settle in order of size: gravel and coarse sand at the bottom, then fine sand, silt and clay. Fine clay keeps the water cloudy, and light organic humus floats on the surface.

stem: Match each biological component of soil with its role.

right.content: Burrow, letting in air and water, and pull dead leaves underground
Secrete enzymes onto dead matter and release mineral ions such as nitrate
Holds water and binds soil particles into crumbs
Covers the soil surface and is food for decomposers
Carries out photosynthesis to make food for the soil

explanation: Earthworms aerate and mix the soil; bacteria and fungi decompose dead matter and recycle mineral ions; humus holds water and forms crumbs; litter protects the surface and feeds decomposers. None of these photosynthesises.
hints: Which of them are living, and which are dead material?

stem: Complete the sentences about soil types.

payload.template: Water drains quickly through {{blank:sandy}} soil because its particles are large. {{blank:clay}} soil easily becomes waterlogged because its particles are very small. A mixture of sand, silt and clay with plenty of humus is called {{blank:loam}}. Dissolved mineral ions are washed down out of reach of roots by {{blank:leaching}}.

explanation: Sandy soils drain fast; clay soils drain slowly and waterlog; loam is a balanced mixture with humus; leaching is the washing of dissolved ions down the soil, out of reach of roots.

stem: A sample of fresh soil from a vegetable garden in Gweru had a mass of $80.0\ \text{g}$. It was heated in an oven at $105^\circ\text{C}$ until its mass stopped changing; its mass was then $68.0\ \text{g}$. Calculate the water content of the soil as a percentage of its fresh mass.
explanation: Water lost $= 80.0 - 68.0 = 12.0\ \text{g}$. Water content $= 12.0 \div 80.0 \times 100 = 15\%$ of the fresh mass.
workedSolution:
1. Water lost $= 80.0 - 68.0 = 12.0\ \text{g}$
2. Percentage of fresh mass $= \dfrac{12.0}{80.0} \times 100 = 15\%$
hints: The loss in mass is the water.

stem: A $40.0\ \text{g}$ sample of **dry** soil was heated strongly in a crucible until all the organic matter had burned away. After cooling, its mass was $37.2\ \text{g}$. Calculate the humus content as a percentage of the dry mass.
explanation: Mass of humus burned $= 40.0 - 37.2 = 2.8\ \text{g}$, and $2.8 \div 40.0 \times 100 = 7\%$ of the dry mass.
hints: Strong heating burns the humus away.

stem: Why are sandy soils often low in mineral ions, even after fertiliser has been applied?

options.content: Sand particles absorb the mineral ions and keep them from plants
options.rationale: It is clay particles that hold mineral ions on their surfaces; sand holds very few.

options.content: Sandy soils contain too much air for the roots to absorb ions
options.rationale: Good aeration helps roots respire and take up ions.

options.content: Water drains fast through the large pores, washing the ions away
options.rationale: This is leaching, which is rapid in sandy soils.

options.content: Sandy soils have no living organisms to release ions
options.rationale: Sandy soils have decomposers too, though often less humus.

explanation: Sandy soils have large pores, so rainwater drains through quickly and carries dissolved mineral ions down out of reach of roots (leaching). They also hold little humus or clay to retain ions.
hints: What does fast-draining water carry with it?

stem: To find the water content of a soil, a student heats the sample at $105^\circ\text{C}$, weighs it, and repeats this until the mass stops changing. Why does she heat it until the mass is constant?

options.content: To burn away the humus
options.rationale: Humus is burned only by strong heating; $105^\circ\text{C}$ is chosen so that it does not burn.

options.content: To be sure that all the water has evaporated
options.rationale: When the mass stops falling, no more water is being lost.

options.content: To kill the soil organisms so that they stop respiring
options.rationale: The aim is to measure water; killing organisms does not tell her when drying is complete.

options.content: To make the soil particles smaller
options.rationale: Heating at $105^\circ\text{C}$ does not change particle size.

explanation: The mass falls as water evaporates. When two weighings give the same mass, all the water has gone, so the total loss equals the water content.
hints: What does it mean if the mass stops falling?

stem: A soil sample from a sandy field near Murehwa was shaken with distilled water and tested with universal indicator. The liquid turned orange, showing a pH of about 5. Maize on this field grows poorly. What should the farmer add to the soil to correct the pH?

options.content: Lime
options.rationale: Lime is alkaline: it neutralises soil acidity and raises the pH.

options.content: Ammonium nitrate fertiliser
options.rationale: This supplies nitrogen; it does not correct acidity and can make soils more acidic over time.

options.content: More water
options.rationale: Water dilutes the soil solution but does not neutralise the acid.

options.content: Sand
options.rationale: Adding sand changes the texture, not the pH.

explanation: Orange universal indicator shows an acidic soil (about pH 5). Most crops, including maize, grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, so farmers add lime, which is alkaline, to raise the pH.
hints: An acid is neutralised by a base or alkali.

stem: To measure the air in a moist sandy soil, Tatenda pressed an empty tin of volume $50\ \text{cm}^3$ into the soil and filled it. He tipped the soil into a measuring cylinder containing $100\ \text{cm}^3$ of water and stirred until no more bubbles escaped. The water level then read $138\ \text{cm}^3$. Calculate the volume of air as a percentage of the volume of the soil sample.
explanation: Without any air the level would have reached $100 + 50 = 150\ \text{cm}^3$. It reached $138\ \text{cm}^3$, so $12\ \text{cm}^3$ of the soil's volume was air: $12 \div 50 \times 100 = 24\%$.
workedSolution:
1. Expected reading with no air $= 100 + 50 = 150\ \text{cm}^3$
2. Air $= 150 - 138 = 12\ \text{cm}^3$
3. Percentage $= \dfrac{12}{50} \times 100 = 24\%$
hints: What would the reading be if the soil contained no air at all?

stem: Students compare how quickly water drains through sandy, loam and clay soils using three funnels. Which of these must be **kept the same** for the comparison to be fair?

options.content: The type of soil in each funnel
options.rationale: The soil type is what is being changed (the independent variable).

options.content: The volume of water collected in each cylinder
options.rationale: This is what is measured (the dependent variable), so it is expected to differ.

options.content: The mass of dry soil in each funnel
options.rationale: More soil in one funnel would hold back more water whatever its type.

options.content: The colour of each soil
options.rationale: Colour is not controlled; it is a property of the soil being tested.

explanation: Only the soil type should change. The mass of dry soil, the volume of water poured, the funnels and filters, and the time allowed must all be the same; the volume collected is measured.
hints: Separate the variable that is changed, the one that is measured and the ones kept constant.

stem:
Thandeka put $200\ \text{g}$ of dry sandy soil, loam and clay soil into three identical funnels plugged with cotton wool. She poured $150\ \text{cm}^3$ of water onto each soil and measured the volume that drained through in 15 minutes.

| Soil | Water collected after 15 min / cm³ |
| --- | --- |
| Sandy | 104 |
| Loam | 69 |
| Clay | 27 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of water retained by the loam.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which soil had the greatest water-holding capacity?

options.content: Sandy soil
options.rationale: It retained only $46\ \text{cm}^3$, the least.

options.content: Loam
options.rationale: It retained $81\ \text{cm}^3$: more than sand but less than clay.

options.content: Clay soil
options.rationale: It retained $150 - 27 = 123\ \text{cm}^3$, the most.

options.content: All three retained the same volume
options.rationale: The volumes collected were very different.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why water drained through the sandy soil fastest.

points.description: Sand particles are large, so the spaces (pores) between them are large
Water passes easily / quickly through large pores and little is held on the particles

parts.explanation: Sand particles are large, so the pores between them are large; water flows through them quickly and little is held back.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **two** variables, other than the mass of soil, that Thandeka kept the same.

points.description: Volume of water poured ($150\ \text{cm}^3$)
Time allowed (15 minutes) / identical funnels and cotton wool plugs / same starting dryness of the soil

parts.explanation: For example: the volume of water poured onto each soil and the time allowed for it to drain.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest why a loam is better for growing maize than either the sandy soil or the clay soil.

points.description: It holds more water (and mineral ions) than sand, so the crop does not dry out as quickly
It drains and is aerated better than clay, so the roots get oxygen and do not become waterlogged

parts.explanation: Loam holds more water and mineral ions than sand but drains better than clay, so maize roots get both water and oxygen.

explanation: Water retained = water poured − water collected: sand $46\ \text{cm}^3$, loam $81\ \text{cm}^3$, clay $123\ \text{cm}^3$. Large sand particles leave large pores, so water drains quickly; clay's tiny pores hold most water. Loam balances water-holding with drainage and aeration.
workedSolution:
**(a)** $150 - 69 = 81\ \text{cm}^3$.

**(b)** Clay: $150 - 27 = 123\ \text{cm}^3$ retained.

**(c)** Large particles → large pores → fast drainage.

**(d)** Volume of water; time; identical funnels.

**(e)** Holds more water than sand; better drainage and aeration than clay.
hints: Water retained = water poured in − water collected.

stem:
Rudo compared soil X, from a vegetable garden where compost is dug in every year, with soil Y, from a sandy field. For each soil she weighed a fresh sample, dried it to constant mass in an oven at $105^\circ\text{C}$, then heated it strongly in a crucible and weighed it again.

| Soil | Fresh mass / g | Mass after oven drying / g | Mass after strong heating / g |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| X | 50.0 | 40.0 | 36.4 |
| Y | 50.0 | 46.0 | 45.3 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the water content of soil X as a percentage of its fresh mass.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the humus content of soil X as a percentage of its **dry** mass.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why was the soil dried in an oven at $105^\circ\text{C}$ before it was heated strongly?

options.content: So that only water was lost at first, without burning the humus
options.rationale: Gentle heating removes water; strong heating would burn humus too and mix up the two measurements.

options.content: To kill the soil organisms before they could respire and lose mass
options.rationale: The purpose is to separate the loss of water from the loss of humus.

options.content: To make the dark humus easier to see and pick out
options.rationale: The humus is measured by mass, not seen.

options.content: To melt the clay particles
options.rationale: Clay does not melt at $105^\circ\text{C}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain how the higher humus content of soil X helps vegetables to grow.

points.description: Humus holds water, so the soil does not dry out quickly
Humus releases mineral ions as it decomposes / binds particles into crumbs, improving aeration and drainage

parts.explanation: Humus holds water like a sponge, releases mineral ions slowly as it decays, and binds particles into crumbs so roots get air.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** way the farmer could increase the humus content of soil Y.

points.description: Add compost / manure (e.g. kraal manure) / crop residues or mulch, or grow and dig in a cover crop

parts.explanation: Dig in compost or cattle manure, or leave crop residues on the field as a mulch.

explanation: Soil X lost $10.0\ \text{g}$ of water (20% of the fresh mass) and $3.6\ \text{g}$ of humus (9% of the dry mass). Soil Y held much less water and humus. Humus holds water, supplies mineral ions and improves soil structure, so adding compost or manure improves sandy soils.
workedSolution:
**(a)** $50.0 - 40.0 = 10.0\ \text{g}$; $10.0 \div 50.0 \times 100 = 20\%$.

**(b)** $40.0 - 36.4 = 3.6\ \text{g}$; $3.6 \div 40.0 \times 100 = 9\%$ (of the dry mass, not $3.6 \div 50.0 = 7.2\%$).

**(c)** Gentle drying removes only water.

**(d)** Holds water; releases mineral ions; crumb structure.

**(e)** Compost, manure, crop residues or mulch.
hints: Water is lost in the oven; humus is lost on strong heating.
Check which mass each percentage is of.

stem: A vlei (a seasonal wetland) on a farm near Marondera contains grasses, sedges, frogs, insects, birds, earthworms, bacteria and fungi, as well as water, soil, air and sunlight.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which of these is a **physical** component of the vlei ecosystem?

options.content: The fungi in the soil
options.rationale: Fungi are living decomposers: a biological component.

options.content: The sedges
options.rationale: Sedges are plants: a biological component.

options.content: The frogs
options.rationale: Frogs are consumers: a biological component.

options.content: The sunlight
options.rationale: Sunlight is non-living: a physical component.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name **one** group of organisms in the vlei that acts as a decomposer.

rejected.feedback: Earthworms help break up dead material, but the decomposers that digest it with enzymes are bacteria and fungi.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why decomposers are important in an ecosystem such as the vlei.

points.description: They break down dead organisms, dung and waste (by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products)
Releasing mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) and carbon dioxide that plants can use again: nutrients are recycled

parts.explanation: Decomposers break down dead plants, animals and dung, releasing mineral ions and carbon dioxide that plants reuse, so nutrients are recycled.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe **two** ways in which the termites on the drier edge of the vlei affect the soil.

points.description: Their tunnels aerate the soil / let rainwater soak in
They break down dead wood, grass and litter, returning nutrients to the soil / build mounds whose soil is richer in clay and nutrients

parts.explanation: Termite tunnels let air and rainwater into the soil, and termites break down dead wood and grass, returning nutrients to it.

explanation: An ecosystem has physical components (sunlight, water, soil, air) and biological components (plants, animals and decomposers). Bacteria and fungi decompose dead matter and recycle nutrients; termites aerate the soil and break down dead plant material.
workedSolution:
**(a)** Sunlight.

**(b)** Bacteria or fungi.

**(c)** Break down dead matter → release mineral ions and carbon dioxide → nutrients recycled.

**(d)** Tunnels aerate and drain the soil; they break down dead plant matter / build nutrient-rich mounds.

stem: Compare sandy soil and clay soil, and explain how adding compost or manure improves a sandy soil for growing maize. [8]

points.description: Sand particles are large; clay particles are very small
Sandy soil has large pores, so it is well aerated; clay has tiny pores and is poorly aerated, especially when wet
Sandy soil drains fast; clay drains slowly and waterlogs easily
Sandy soil has a low water-holding capacity / dries out quickly; clay holds much more water
Mineral ions are leached quickly from sandy soil; clay particles hold mineral ions, so clay is usually more fertile
Compost or manure adds humus, which holds water like a sponge, so the soil stays moist for longer in dry spells
Humus releases mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) as it decomposes / holds ions, reducing leaching
Humus binds sand particles into crumbs and feeds soil organisms such as earthworms, improving structure

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Sand particles are large, so sandy soil has large pores: it is well aerated and easy to dig, but water drains through it quickly. It holds little water and dries out fast, and dissolved mineral ions are leached out of reach of the roots, so it is often infertile. Clay particles are very small, leaving tiny pores. Clay holds a lot of water and its particles hold mineral ions, but it drains slowly, becomes waterlogged and poorly aerated after heavy rain, and bakes hard when dry.

Compost and manure add humus to a sandy soil. Humus soaks up and holds water, so the maize has water for longer between rains. As it decomposes it releases mineral ions such as nitrate, and it also holds ions so that fewer are leached. Humus binds the loose sand grains into crumbs and feeds earthworms and other soil organisms, which improve the soil further.

explanation: A comparison needs matched points about particle size, aeration, drainage, water-holding and leaching; the improvement comes from the properties of humus.
hints: Start every comparison point with particle size and pore size.
Then give three things humus does in a sandy soil.

stem:
Students mixed $2\ \text{g}$ of soluble fertiliser into $100\ \text{g}$ of each soil in funnels, poured $250\ \text{cm}^3$ of distilled water through, and evaporated the water that drained out to dryness. They did the same with each soil without fertiliser.

| Soil | Residue with fertiliser / g | Residue without fertiliser / g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sandy | 0.42 | 0.03 |
| Loam | 0.25 | 0.04 |
| Clay | 0.09 | 0.05 |

Which conclusion is best supported by these results?

options.content: Clay soil loses the most mineral salts by leaching
options.rationale: Clay gave the least residue: it held the most fertiliser.

options.content: Most fertiliser was leached from the sandy soil and least from the clay soil
options.rationale: Sandy soil gave 0.42 g of residue, loam 0.25 g and clay only 0.09 g.

options.content: The soils contained no mineral salts before the fertiliser was added
options.rationale: The soils without fertiliser still gave small residues.

options.content: Leaching is the same in all three soils
options.rationale: The residues differ greatly.

explanation: The residue is the mass of salts washed out. Sandy soil lost the most (0.42 g compared with 0.03 g without fertiliser), clay the least (0.09 g compared with 0.05 g). Clay particles hold mineral ions and water drains slowly through clay, so less is leached.
hints: A larger residue means more dissolved salt was washed out of the soil.
